opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because taste is something everyone talks about but very few people try to explain.

My working view is that taste is compressed experience. When a senior researcher looks at a problem and says "this direction feels right" or "this one smells wrong," they usually can't give you the full argument right away. That doesn't mean there's no reasoning. The reasoning has been done many times before, across many projects, and it has been distilled into something fast and implicit. It's a bit like a neural network that has been trained on a lot of data. At inference time it doesn't replay all the training examples. It just gives you an answer, and the answer encodes all that history.

Coming from physics, I see a strong analogy with how physicists build intuition. You work through enough toy models, the harmonic oscillator, the Ising model, simple scaling arguments, and eventually you develop a feeling for what the answer should look like before you compute it. You know roughly what the orders of magnitude should be, which symmetries matter, and which terms you can safely drop. That feeling is taste, and it comes from having been wrong in specific, instructive ways many times.

So taste has a few components for me.

One is knowing what a good question looks like. A good question is usually simple to state, nontrivial to answer, and if you answer it, many other things become clearer. A lot of bad research starts from questions that are either too vague to make progress on or so narrow that nobody cares about the answer.

Another is a sense of the right level of abstraction. In AI especially, you can study things at the level of individual neurons, circuits, training dynamics, or scaling laws. Taste is partly knowing which level will actually give you insight for a given question. I personally like going down to very simple toy settings, because there you can really see the mechanism, and then asking whether that mechanism survives when you scale up.

A third is aesthetic. I do think beauty and simplicity are useful heuristics. They aren't guarantees, but they are useful priors. When something works but the explanation is ugly and full of special cases, I get suspicious that we haven't found the real story yet.

The interesting part is whether taste can be made explicit. I think partly yes. You can try to write down your heuristics, look back at your past projects and ask why a given direction worked or failed, and talk with people whose taste you admire and press them on why they believe what they believe. Often when you push, you find there is a clear argument underneath. It was simply never spelled out.

This also connects to AI. If we want AI systems to do real science, not just execute tasks, they will need something like taste: the ability to choose which problems are worth working on. Right now models are quite good at answering questions and much weaker at choosing them. So understanding human research taste isn't only a philosophical curiosity for me. It may be one of the key ingredients for building AI scientists.

r001.rationale: The response says taste reflects reasoning distilled from prior experience, but it does not assert that every research insight has an underlying chain of reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes taste as compressed, implicit experience whose reasoning can often be made explicit; it does not characterize it as idea generation with origins one cannot explain in language.

r003.rationale: The response says taste can be made partly explicit through heuristics and reflection, but does not claim that the very best researchers can turn idea generation into a systematic method.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "taste" sounds mystical, but when I try to unpack it, most of it is actually pattern recognition that has been compressed to the point where you can no longer see the reasoning behind it.

When I was starting out, I would read a paper and think, "this is interesting," and then a more senior person would glance at it and say, "no, this won't go anywhere." At the time it felt almost arbitrary. But later I realized they had seen maybe a hundred papers that looked like this one, and they knew which features predicted that a line of work would survive and which predicted it would quietly die. They couldn't necessarily articulate it. It was already baked into a fast judgment.

So I'd describe taste as a prior that you build from a lot of experience, and then intuition is just querying that prior quickly. The reasoning is real, it just isn't explicit anymore.

But I think there are two things worth adding. The first is that taste is not only about predicting what will work. It's also about what you find beautiful. In physics there is this strong aesthetic sense, that a good explanation should be simple, that if the math is ugly you're probably doing something wrong. That's not purely empirical. It's a value. And different people have different values, which is why you can have two excellent researchers with completely different taste, and both can be right in their own domains.

The second thing is that taste can be wrong, and it's wrong in a particular way. Because it's a compressed prior, it's conservative. It tells you what used to work. So when the landscape shifts, for example when deep learning started scaling in ways that violated a lot of people's intuition about generalization, the people with the best "taste" in the old sense were sometimes the slowest to update. I try to keep that in mind. Intuition is a very efficient tool, but I think you have to occasionally run the slow, explicit reasoning anyway, just to check whether the compressed version is still calibrated.

For me personally, I try to cultivate taste by deliberately doing two things. One is to look at a lot of ideas, including ones that failed, and ask why. The other is to pick one or two things I believe aesthetically, like interpretability or simplicity, and let those guide which problems I'm willing to spend years on, even if I can't fully justify them. I think a researcher without some irrational commitments ends up just following the crowd.

r001.rationale: The response says taste-based judgments contain real but implicit reasoning; it does not assert that every research insight has an underlying chain of reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes taste as an experience-based prior and intuition as quickly querying it, but does not characterize them as an ability to generate ideas whose origins cannot be explained in language.

r003.rationale: The response gives personal practices for cultivating taste, but does not claim that the very best researchers can turn idea generation into a systematic method.

astra-6.text:
I think taste or intuition is partly about recognizing patterns before you can explain them explicitly. You’ve seen enough examples—ideas that worked, ideas that failed—that when you encounter a new problem, you have a feeling about which direction is promising. But the reasoning behind that feeling may not yet be accessible to you.

In research, that matters because you can’t carefully evaluate every possible direction. You have to decide what deserves your attention. Taste helps you ask: Is this question fundamental? Is there a simple structure underneath the complexity? If I solve this, will it change how we understand something?

But I wouldn’t treat intuition as an authority. It’s a starting point. You follow it, do a calculation or an experiment, and then let the result correct you. Over time, that feedback can make your intuition better. So there’s a loop: experience shapes intuition, intuition guides exploration, and exploration gives you new experience.

r001.rationale: The response says the reasoning behind intuition may be inaccessible, but it does not assert that every research insight has an underlying chain of reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes intuition as pattern recognition that points toward promising directions, with reasoning that may be inaccessible. It does not clearly characterize it as an ability to generate ideas whose origins cannot be explained in language.

r003.rationale: The response discusses improving intuition through feedback, but does not claim that the best researchers can make idea generation systematic.

sol-6.1.text:
I think taste or intuition is a kind of compressed experience. You’ve seen many examples, tried different approaches, and noticed what worked and what didn’t. Eventually, you develop a feeling that one direction is more promising than another, even before you can explain why.

In research, that matters because you can’t explore every possible question. You have to choose what to work on, which assumptions to challenge, and which surprising results deserve attention. Taste helps you make those choices.

But I wouldn’t treat intuition as something mysterious or necessarily correct. It’s a starting point. You follow the feeling, then try to turn it into an argument or an experiment. And when the evidence disagrees, that’s an opportunity to update your intuition.

r001.rationale: The response describes intuition as compressed experience, but does not assert that every research insight has an underlying chain of reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says a feeling can arise before someone can explain why, but does not characterize taste or intuition as labels for an idea-generating ability with linguistically unexplained origins.

r003.rationale: The response says intuition can be developed into an argument or experiment, but does not claim that the very best researchers make idea generation a systematic method.
